lesson.menu_desc: Presenting next quarter and defending the one thing you decided not to do -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- Plans and Priorities
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Marcos Aurélio Miranda de Moura | Lesson 5 -- Plans and Priorities

listenings.text: Today I am going to cover three points, and then I am going to ask you for one approval. First, the priority. We are going to put the whole budget behind the workshop programme and nothing behind the trade fair this year. That is a trade-off and I want to name it as a trade-off, because we are giving up something real. Second, the timeline. The proposal goes out to the distributors in the first week of October, the rollout starts in November, and the first milestone is thirty per cent coverage by the end of January. Third, what we are not going to do. We are going to postpone the packaging change to the second half of the year. It is a good project and it is not this year's project. And the approval I need today is the budget, because the deadline for the distributor contracts is the fifteenth.

I sit in a lot of planning meetings, and the ones that work all do the same small thing at the start. They say what they are not going to do. Everybody arrives with a list of what they are going to build, and every list is longer than the year. So the room nods, the plan gets approved, and eight months later somebody works out that three of the five things never had a chance. The plan that survives is the one that names the trade-off out loud in the first two minutes. We are going to do this. We are not going to do that. Here is what we lose by not doing it, and here is why we are prepared to lose it. It takes thirty seconds and it changes the whole conversation, because the room stops arguing about whether the plan is optimistic and starts arguing about whether the trade-off is the right one, which is the argument you actually want.

Every planning season the same question comes back in this industry, and it is a hard one. Do you put the money where the volume already is, or where the growth is going to come from? The volume is in the big distributors, who buy in quantity, pay on time and give up almost no margin. The growth, in almost every market we looked at, is in the small independent workshop, which buys ten litres at a time and decides what to recommend to the driver standing in front of it. The companies that chose the workshop had two very slow years and then a very good third one. The companies that chose the distributor had three comfortable years and are now finding that somebody else owns the conversation at the counter. Neither choice was wrong on the day it was made. Both of them took three years to prove anything, which is longer than most marketing directors stay in the job.
